To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we report the first observation and explanation of the effects of competing $\left(\chi\right)^{\left(\right. 2 \left.\right)}$ nonlinearities on quantum states, and that we report new classical signatures that are expected to have significant practical implications.

competition between various $\Chi^{(2)} $ processes imposes limits on power generation and squeezing in nonlinear optics, and that these limits are observable as a clamping of the power of the second harmonic and the generation of nondegenerate visible frequencies.

the quantum and classical signatures of competition between $\chi^{(3)}$ and $\chi^{(4)}$ are observed for the first time in an optical parametric oscillator, that the quantum effects are due to a competition between upconversion and down conversion processes, that the classical effects are clamping of the output power and generation of nondegenerate visible frequencies, that the classical and quantum effects are due in part to competition, and that competition limits both power generation and quantum squeezing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation, manipulation, and measurement of quantum light.
the quantum properties of optical nonlinearities.
the generation, detection, and application of optical quantum states, and with the development of new quantum optical techniques.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the quantum and classical signatures of competing $\chi^2$ nonlinearities have been reported for the first time.

the quantum signature is the first experimental observation of the effects of $\chi^{(3)}$ competition on $\chi^{(1)}$ and $\chi^{(5)}$, the classical signature is the first observation of nondegenerate frequency generation in the visible, and that both signatures are the first observations of the quantum effects associated with $\chi^{(n)}$ competition.
the quantum signature of the $\chi^{(3)}$ nonlinearities is a quantum signature of the nonlinearities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the quantum effects of competition are observable and that competition is an important effect in classical nonlinear optical systems.
the $\chi^{(3)}$ nonlinearity of the optical medium is the source of the quantum effects.
the quantum theory of the nonlinear optical process is now sufficiently advanced to allow for the design of new devices with novel quantum properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
competition between various $\Chi$ processes in nonlinear crystals is a general effect that can lead to unexpected behavior.

$\chi^{(3)}$ effects, which are usually considered negligible in the context of $\chi^{(4)}$ and $\chi^{(5)}$ systems, are in fact important in $\chi^{(6)}$ systems, where they can lead to unexpected effects.
the $\chi^{(3)}$ nonlinearity is not the only nonlinear effect that can limit power generation in a $\chi^{(4)}$ system.
